overview.title: Tensor slicing in NumPy and the samples axis
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.subsection: 2.2.6 Manipulating tensors in NumPy / 2.2.7 The notion of data batches
overview.main_topic: Selecting sub-tensors with NumPy slicing syntax (start:stop per axis, `:` for a whole axis, negative indices), and the convention that axis 0 of any data tensor is the samples axis along which data is cut into batches.
overview.central_idea: A slice like `train_images[10:100, 7:-7, 7:-7]` picks a contiguous range along every axis independently; the first axis of every data tensor indexes samples, and deep learning models consume those samples in fixed-size batches rather than all at once.
overview.importance: Nearly every data-preparation line you will write in Keras is a slice along one or more axes. Knowing that axis 0 is the samples axis is what makes `train_images[10:100]` meaningful, and it is the reason mini-batch training (introduced in 2.4.3) works by indexing contiguous chunks of that axis.
learning_objectives: Write a NumPy slice that selects a range of samples, or a rectangular pixel patch, from a rank-3 image tensor and predict its shape.
Explain why `train_images[10:100]`, `train_images[10:100, :, :]` and `train_images[10:100, 0:28, 0:28]` are all equivalent.
Use negative indices to crop relative to the end of an axis (e.g. `7:-7`).
State the samples-axis convention (axis 0) and why deep learning models process data in batches.

summary:
This page closes section 2.2's tour of tensor attributes with two short subsections.

**2.2.6 Manipulating tensors in NumPy.** Selecting elements of a tensor is called *tensor slicing*. The authors start from the familiar `train_images[i]` (one digit along the first axis) and generalize. `train_images[10:100]` selects digits #10 through #99 (the stop index 100 is excluded) and returns a tensor of shape `(90, 28, 28)`. This is shown to be exactly equivalent to the more explicit `train_images[10:100, :, :]` and to `train_images[10:100, 0:28, 0:28]`: each axis gets its own `start:stop` range, and a bare `:` means "the whole axis". From there, any rectangular sub-tensor can be chosen. Selecting the bottom-right 14 × 14 pixels of *all* images is `train_images[:, 14:, 14:]`. Negative indices count from the end of an axis, as in Python lists, so a centered 14 × 14 patch is `train_images[:, 7:-7, 7:-7]` (rows and columns 7 through 20).

**2.2.7 The notion of data batches.** Two conventions are stated. First, in every data tensor you will meet in deep learning, axis 0 is the *samples axis* (for MNIST, a sample is one digit image). Second, deep learning models do not process the whole dataset at once; they break it into small *batches* of samples of a fixed size. The page ends by starting a concrete example with a batch size of 128, which continues on p.50 (`train_images[:128]`, then `[128:256]`, then the *n*th batch, and the term *batch axis*).

There are no formulas or figures on this page; the content is the slicing syntax itself and the samples-axis / batch convention that the rest of the book relies on (for example, `fit()` iterating over mini-batches of 128 in the first example on p.44, and stochastic gradient descent on p.67).

paragraphs.excerpt: In the previous example, we selected a specific digit alongside the first axis
paragraphs.what_it_says: Writing `train_images[i]` picked one digit along the first axis. Picking specific elements of a tensor is called *tensor slicing*, and the subsection will walk through the slicing operations NumPy arrays support.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Indexing with a single integer is the simplest slice: it fixes a position on axis 0 and returns everything below it (a 28 × 28 matrix for MNIST). The general operation lets you specify a range on *each* axis.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Slicing is how you pull out a validation split, a mini-batch, a crop or a single example; it is the most common tensor manipulation in practical code.
paragraphs.technical_idea: A NumPy index expression has one entry per axis (missing trailing entries default to `:`). An integer entry removes that axis from the result; a `start:stop` entry keeps the axis but restricts its range.

terminology.meaning: Selecting a sub-tensor by giving an index or index range along one or more axes.
Axis 0 of the tensor; for `train_images` it indexes the 60,000 digit images.

connections: p.48: `train_images[4]` was used (with Matplotlib) to display the fourth digit; that is the single-index case generalized here.

paragraphs.excerpt: The following example selects digits #10 to #100 (#100 isn’t included)
paragraphs.what_it_says: `train_images[10:100]` selects digits #10 up to but not including #100, producing an array of shape `(90, 28, 28)`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Python ranges are half-open: `start` is included, `stop` is excluded, so the count is `stop - start = 90`. Only axis 0 is restricted; the two image axes keep their full 28 entries.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The half-open convention is what lets consecutive batches `[0:128]`, `[128:256]`, … tile the dataset with no overlap and no gaps (p.50).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Shape bookkeeping: slicing a `(60000, 28, 28)` tensor on axis 0 with a range of length 90 gives `(90, 28, 28)`; the rank (3) is unchanged because a range, unlike an integer index, never drops an axis.

terminology.meaning: `a:b` includes index a and excludes index b, so it has b − a elements.

connections: p.47: `train_images.shape` is `(60000, 28, 28)`, the tensor being sliced here.

paragraphs.excerpt: It’s equivalent to this more detailed notation, which specifies a start index
paragraphs.what_it_says: The same slice can be written with an explicit `start:stop` for every axis: `train_images[10:100, :, :]` and `train_images[10:100, 0:28, 0:28]` both give `(90, 28, 28)`. A lone `:` selects the entire axis.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each axis is sliced independently; omitting an axis or writing `:` means "take all of it". The three spellings are literally the same operation, which the page's margin callouts emphasize ("Equivalent to the previous example", "Also equivalent to the previous example").
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Seeing the explicit form makes clear that a slice is a *per-axis* range, which is the mental model you need for the pixel-crop examples that follow and for every shape you will later read in a Keras model.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Index tuple `(10:100, 0:28, 0:28)` → output shape `(100−10, 28−0, 28−0) = (90, 28, 28)`. In general, for slice `a_k:b_k` on axis k the output size on that axis is `b_k − a_k` (when within bounds and step 1).

terminology.meaning: Selects every index along that axis; equivalent to `0:n` where n is the axis length.

paragraphs.excerpt: In general, you may select slices between any two indices along each tensor
paragraphs.what_it_says: Any two indices may bound the slice on each axis. To get the bottom-right 14 × 14 pixels of every image: `train_images[:, 14:, 14:]`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: `:` on axis 0 keeps all 60,000 images; `14:` on the row axis keeps rows 14..27 (the bottom half); `14:` on the column axis keeps columns 14..27 (the right half). The result has shape `(60000, 14, 14)`. An omitted `stop` defaults to the end of the axis.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the first example of slicing the *non*-sample axes, which is how you crop, patch or window images in preprocessing and data augmentation.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Rows in an image array run top to bottom with index 0 at the top, so rows 14–27 are the lower half; columns run left to right, so 14–27 is the right half. Together: bottom-right quadrant.
connections: p.51: images are usually stored as rank-4 `(samples, height, width, channels)` tensors; the same slicing applies with one more axis.

paragraphs.excerpt: It’s also possible to use negative indices. Much like negative indices in Python
paragraphs.what_it_says: Negative indices count from the end of an axis, as in Python lists. A centered 14 × 14 crop is `train_images[:, 7:-7, 7:-7]`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: `-7` means `28 − 7 = 21`, so `7:-7` is the same as `7:21`: rows and columns 7 through 20, i.e. 14 pixels, leaving a 7-pixel margin on every side. The result again has shape `(60000, 14, 14)`.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Negative indices let you write crops that do not depend on knowing the axis length, which keeps preprocessing code reusable across image sizes.
paragraphs.technical_idea: For an axis of length n, index `-k` is translated to `n − k`. Output size on each cropped axis: `(28 − 7) − 7 = 14`.

terminology.meaning: A position measured from the end of the axis: `-1` is the last element, `-7` is seven from the end.

paragraphs.excerpt: In general, the first axis (axis 0, because indexing starts at 0) in all
paragraphs.what_it_says: In all data tensors you will see in deep learning, the first axis (axis 0) is the *samples axis*. For MNIST, samples are digit images.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Whatever the data modality, position 0 of the shape tuple counts examples. This is why `train_images[10:100]` selected 90 *digits* and why `(60000, 28, 28)` reads as "60,000 samples of 28 × 28".
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is a convention, but one every layer, loss and training loop in Keras assumes; the shape tables on p.50-51 (`(samples, features)`, `(samples, timesteps, features)`, `(samples, height, width, channels)`) all begin with it.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Because axis 0 is samples, operations that must treat each example independently (loss per sample, batching, shuffling) all act along axis 0, while the model's weights act on the remaining axes.

terminology.meaning: Axis 0 of a data tensor; each index along it is one example (also called the samples dimension).

connections: p.50: the same axis is called the *batch axis* once you look at one batch at a time.
p.50-51: real-world data tensors all have `samples` first.

paragraphs.excerpt: In addition, deep learning models don’t process an entire dataset at once;
paragraphs.what_it_says: Models do not process a whole dataset at once; they split it into small *batches*, groups of samples of a fixed size. The page starts a concrete MNIST example with batch size 128 (the code continues on p.50).
paragraphs.what_it_means: A batch is simply a slice along the samples axis: `train_images[:128]` is the first batch, `train_images[128:256]` the second, and batch n is `train_images[128 * n:128 * (n + 1)]` (p.50). Fixed size means every batch tensor has the same shape, `(128, 28, 28)`.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Batching is the bridge between the slicing syntax just learned and the training algorithm: mini-batch SGD (p.67) draws one batch, computes the loss and gradient on it, updates the weights, and moves to the next batch. The first example already used `batch_size=128` in `fit()` on p.44.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: processing in batches bounds memory use (a batch, not the dataset, must fit on the accelerator) and gives a gradient estimate that is cheap yet reasonably accurate; the trade-off is discussed on p.67-69.

terminology.meaning: A group of samples of fixed size (here 128) processed together in one step.
The number of samples per batch; 128 in this example.

connections: p.67: stochastic gradient descent draws random batches to compute gradients.

concepts.name: Tensor slicing
concepts.definition: Selecting a sub-tensor by specifying an index or an index range (`start:stop`) along each axis of a tensor.
concepts.intuition: Think of the tensor as a stack of images; slicing lets you take a contiguous run of images from the stack, and optionally a rectangular window out of each image, in one expression.
concepts.technical: A NumPy index has one entry per axis. An integer fixes that axis (removing it); `a:b` keeps indices a ≤ i < b; `:` keeps the whole axis; omitted trailing axes default to `:`; a negative bound `-k` means `n − k` for axis length n. Output size on a sliced axis is `b − a`.
concepts.significance: Every batch, crop, validation split or feature selection in practical code is a slice; the page's examples (`[10:100]`, `[:, 14:, 14:]`, `[:, 7:-7, 7:-7]`) cover the three patterns you will reuse constantly.
concepts.misconception: That `train_images[10:100]` includes image #100. It does not: the stop index is excluded, giving 90 images.

concepts.name: Samples axis (axis 0)
concepts.definition: The first axis of every data tensor in deep learning, along which individual examples (samples) are indexed.
concepts.intuition: The shape tuple reads "how many examples, then what each example looks like": `(60000, 28, 28)` is 60,000 examples of 28 × 28.
concepts.technical: Indexing starts at 0, so the samples axis is axis 0. Slices along it select examples; the remaining axes describe one example. When the tensor is one batch, the same axis is called the batch axis (p.50).
concepts.significance: The whole Keras API presupposes this: layer input shapes omit it, `fit()` iterates over it, and per-sample losses are averaged over it.
concepts.example: For MNIST, `train_images[i]` is sample i, a `(28, 28)` image; for the actuarial dataset on p.50, `(100000, 3)` is 100,000 people each described by 3 features.
concepts.misconception: That the samples axis is just another axis. It is special by convention: models never apply weights along it; they treat each index as an independent example.

concepts.name: Data batch
concepts.definition: A group of samples of fixed size (the batch size) that a model processes together in one step, obtained by slicing the samples axis.
concepts.intuition: Instead of reading the whole textbook before taking any notes, the model reads 128 pages at a time and updates its notes after each chunk.
concepts.technical: With batch size 128, batch n is `train_images[128 * n:128 * (n + 1)]`, of shape `(128, 28, 28)` (p.50). Each training step computes the loss and its gradient on one batch and updates the weights (p.67).
concepts.significance: Batching makes training feasible on large datasets (memory) and is the "stochastic" in stochastic gradient descent.
concepts.example: `train_images[:128]` is the first batch; `train_images[128:256]` is the second.
concepts.misconception: That a model sees the entire dataset at every update. It sees one batch per update; an epoch is one pass over all batches.

code.title: Selecting digits #10 to #99 along the samples axis
code.what_it_does: Takes a contiguous run of 90 images (indices 10 through 99) from the 60,000-image training tensor and prints the resulting shape.

line_explanations.explanation: Slice only the first axis with the half-open range 10:100. The other two axes are implicitly `:` (kept whole).
The shape shows 100 − 10 = 90 samples, each still 28 × 28. The rank stays 3 because a range slice never drops an axis.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: `train_images`, a `uint8` tensor of shape `(60000, 28, 28)` (p.47-48). Output: `my_slice`, shape `(90, 28, 28)`, same dtype.
code.algorithm: Index translation: for axis 0 keep positions i with 10 ≤ i < 100; for axes 1 and 2 keep everything.
code.theory_link: Demonstrates that axis 0 is the samples axis: a range on it selects whole examples.
pitfalls: Beyond the book: NumPy basic slices are *views*, not copies. Modifying `my_slice` in place would modify `train_images` too; use `.copy()` if you need independence.

code.title: The same slice written with explicit ranges on every axis
code.original_code:
>>> my_slice = train_images[10:100, :, :]
>>> my_slice.shape
(90, 28, 28)
>>> my_slice = train_images[10:100, 0:28, 0:28]
>>> my_slice.shape
(90, 28, 28)
code.what_it_does: Shows two more verbose spellings of the previous slice. The page's margin callouts label them "Equivalent to the previous example" and "Also equivalent to the previous example".

line_explanations.explanation: `:` on axes 1 and 2 explicitly selects the entire 28-pixel height and width; the result is identical to `train_images[10:100]`.
`0:28` is the fully explicit form of `:` for an axis of length 28; again `(90, 28, 28)`.

code.algorithm: One `start:stop` per axis; output size on axis k is `stop_k − start_k`: (100−10, 28−0, 28−0).
code.theory_link: Makes the per-axis nature of slicing explicit, which is what the pixel-cropping examples build on.
pitfalls: Writing `0:28` hard-codes the image size; prefer `:` when you mean "the whole axis" so the code still works for other image sizes.

code.title: Bottom-right 14 × 14 pixels of all images
code.what_it_does: Keeps every image but crops each to its bottom-right quadrant.

line_explanations.explanation: `:` keeps all 60,000 samples; `14:` on the row axis keeps rows 14..27 (bottom half); `14:` on the column axis keeps columns 14..27 (right half). An omitted stop means "to the end". Resulting shape (not printed in the book): `(60000, 14, 14)`.

code.algorithm: Per-axis ranges: axis 0 → all; axis 1 → 14 ≤ r < 28; axis 2 → 14 ≤ c < 28.
code.theory_link: First example of slicing the non-sample axes: cropping is just slicing the height and width axes.

parameters.role: from row/column 14 to the end of the axis

pitfalls: Row index 0 is the top of the image, so `14:` on axis 1 is the *bottom* half, not the top.

code.title: Centered 14 × 14 crop using negative indices
code.what_it_does: Crops every image to the central 14 × 14 patch, leaving a 7-pixel border on each side.

line_explanations.explanation: `-7` is translated to `28 − 7 = 21`, so `7:-7` equals `7:21`: 14 rows (7..20) and 14 columns (7..20). Resulting shape (not printed in the book): `(60000, 14, 14)`.

code.algorithm: Negative bound resolution (`n − k`), then the usual half-open range on each axis.
code.theory_link: Negative indexing behaves exactly as for Python lists, so Python intuition carries over to tensors.

parameters.role: stop: stop 7 rows/columns before the end

pitfalls: A slice like `7:-7` on an axis shorter than 14 silently returns an empty axis (size 0) rather than raising an error.
code.illustrative_code:
import numpy as np
from keras.datasets import mnist
(train_images, _), _ = mnist.load_data()

print(train_images[:, 14:, 14:].shape)    # (60000, 14, 14) bottom-right
print(train_images[:, 7:-7, 7:-7].shape)  # (60000, 14, 14) centered

# Sanity check: negative bound equals n - k
assert np.array_equal(train_images[:, 7:-7, 7:-7],
                      train_images[:, 7:21, 7:21])

# The first two batches of size 128 (continues on p.50)
print(train_images[:128].shape, train_images[128:256].shape)

deeper.title: Reading an index expression axis by axis
deeper.body:
Take `train_images[10:100, 7:-7, 7:-7]` (a combination of the page's examples) on a tensor of shape `(60000, 28, 28)`.

1. **Count the entries.** Three entries, one per axis. If there were fewer, the missing trailing ones would be `:`.
2. **Axis 0, `10:100`.** Keep samples 10..99 → 90 samples.
3. **Axis 1, `7:-7`.** Length is 28, so `-7` → 21; keep rows 7..20 → 14 rows.
4. **Axis 2, `7:-7`.** Same → 14 columns.
5. **Assemble the shape.** `(90, 14, 14)`. The rank is unchanged (3) because every entry is a range; had axis 0 been a plain integer such as `train_images[4]`, that axis would disappear and the result would be `(28, 28)` as on p.48.

The rule of thumb: ranges keep axes, integers remove them, and each axis is handled independently.

deeper.title: Slicing a tensor is like cutting a loaf of sliced bread
deeper.body: Picture `train_images` as a loaf of 60,000 square slices of bread, each 28 × 28 crumbs. `train_images[10:100]` pulls 90 consecutive slices out of the loaf without touching their shape. `train_images[:, 14:, 14:]` keeps every slice but cuts off the top and left crusts, leaving the bottom-right quarter of each. `train_images[:, 7:-7, 7:-7]` trims a 7-crumb crust off all four sides of every slice. Batches of 128 are just the loaf served 128 slices at a time, in order, until the loaf is finished — one *epoch*.

deeper.title: Why the samples axis matters for batching
deeper.body:
The two subsections on this page fit together: because axis 0 is *always* samples, a batch is *always* a slice along axis 0, whatever the data type:

| Data (p.50-51) | Full tensor shape | Batch of 128 |
|---|---|---|
| Vector data | `(samples, features)` | `x[128*n:128*(n+1)]` → `(128, features)` |
| Timeseries | `(samples, timesteps, features)` | `(128, timesteps, features)` |
| Images | `(samples, height, width, channels)` | `(128, height, width, channels)` |
| Video | `(samples, frames, height, width, channels)` | `(128, frames, height, width, channels)` |

The model's layers never see the samples axis as something to learn from; they apply the same weights to every index along it. That is also why Keras lets you leave the batch size unspecified (`None`) in input shapes.

misconceptions.correction: The stop index is excluded, exactly as in Python lists: indices 10..99, i.e. 90 images, shape `(90, 28, 28)`.

misconceptions.claim: Slicing with a range reduces the rank of the tensor.
misconceptions.correction: Only an integer index removes an axis (`train_images[4]` is `(28, 28)`). A range such as `10:100` keeps the axis, so `(60000, 28, 28)` becomes `(90, 28, 28)`, still rank 3.
Row index 0 is the top and column index 0 is the left, so rows and columns 14..27 are the bottom-right quadrant, as the book states.

misconceptions.claim: A deep learning model is fed the entire training set at once.
misconceptions.correction: Models process the data in fixed-size batches (128 here), each a slice along the samples axis; the weights are updated after each batch.

takeaways: Tensor slicing selects a contiguous `start:stop` range on each axis independently; `:` means the whole axis and trailing axes default to `:`.
`train_images[10:100]`, `train_images[10:100, :, :]` and `train_images[10:100, 0:28, 0:28]` are identical and yield shape `(90, 28, 28)`; the stop index is excluded.
Negative indices count from the end: `7:-7` on a 28-long axis is `7:21`, so `train_images[:, 7:-7, 7:-7]` is a centered 14 × 14 crop; `[:, 14:, 14:]` is the bottom-right 14 × 14.
Axis 0 of every data tensor is the samples axis.
Models process data in fixed-size batches (128 in the MNIST example), each of which is a slice along the samples axis.

questions.question: What is the shape of `train_images[10:100]` when `train_images` has shape `(60000, 28, 28)`?
questions.explanation: The range 10:100 is half-open, so it contains 100 − 10 = 90 indices; the other two axes are untouched. (91, 28, 28) wrongly includes index 100; (90, 784) would require a reshape, which slicing does not do; (28, 28) is what a single integer index such as `train_images[4]` returns.

questions.question: Rewrite `train_images[:, 7:-7, 7:-7]` without negative indices, and give the resulting shape.
questions.explanation: On an axis of length 28, `-7` translates to 28 − 7 = 21. Rows and columns 7..20 are kept, 14 of each, for all 60,000 images.

questions.question: Why are `train_images[10:100]`, `train_images[10:100, :, :]` and `train_images[10:100, 0:28, 0:28]` all equivalent?
questions.answer: Because an index expression has one range per axis; omitted trailing axes and `:` both mean "the entire axis", and `0:28` is the explicit form of the whole axis when its length is 28. All three therefore restrict only axis 0 to 10..99.
questions.explanation: The page states that `:` is equivalent to selecting the entire axis and that the detailed notation specifies a start and stop index along each axis; the page's callouts mark both longer forms as equivalent to the first.

questions.question: Which slice selects the bottom-right 14 × 14 pixels of every MNIST image?
questions.explanation: Axis 0 must stay `:` to keep all images; rows 14..27 are the bottom half and columns 14..27 the right half. `train_images[14:, 14:]` would slice the samples axis and the row axis instead; `[:, :14, :14]` is the top-left quadrant; `[:, 14:, :14]` is bottom-left.

questions.question: In deep learning data tensors, which axis is the samples axis, and what is a "sample" in the MNIST example?
questions.answer: Axis 0 (the first axis); in MNIST a sample is one digit image.
questions.explanation: The page states that the first axis, axis 0 because indexing starts at 0, is the samples axis in all data tensors you will come across, and that for MNIST the samples are images of digits.

questions.question: How does the notion of a data batch relate to tensor slicing?
questions.answer: A batch is a fixed-size group of samples, which is exactly a slice along the samples axis: with batch size 128, the first batch is `train_images[:128]`, the next `train_images[128:256]`, and in general `train_images[128 * n:128 * (n + 1)]` (p.50).
questions.explanation: Because axis 0 indexes samples, taking consecutive half-open ranges of length 128 along it partitions the dataset into non-overlapping batches of identical shape `(128, 28, 28)`.

questions.question: Without running code, can you write the slice that keeps the top-left 7 × 7 corner of images #0..#999 and state its shape?
questions.explanation: Range of length 1000 on the samples axis, rows 0..6 and columns 0..6 (top and left, since index 0 is the top-left). If you got this, you have the per-axis slicing rule down; if not, re-read the equivalence examples and the two crop examples on the page.
